endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: 1. Require that internal developers and vendors complete a Model Card (or similar documentation) and Standard Intake Application

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: i) W here a mandated use of AI systems prevents mitigation of risk and harm, the individual or entity issuing the mandate must be assigned all applicable liability.

endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Review various transparency artifacts (e.g., system cards and model cards) for third-party models.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: In part, risk assessment can be facilitated by consulting the risk matrix and the risk–benefit analysis provided in the regulatory files by vendors. However, some risks may not be addressed in such regulatory filings or only become apparent during use.

endorsements.title: Choosing the right artificial intelligence solutions for your radiology department: key factors to consider
endorsements.quote: In addition to the considerations outlined above, we recommend the establishment of a departmental review (or assessment) board specifically for the procurement of AI solutions.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether a standardized AI vendor intake with minimum disclosure and governance review reduces the purchase of undocumented or high-risk tools, and no study documents the hazard itself. Five sources endorse the practice at strengths from may to must, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The support consists of two frameworks, two guidance documents, and one commentary. These sources reflect expert agreement, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect. Certainty stays at no direct evidence until an organization compares review outcomes or adverse events before and after adopting intake.

The multi-society radiology statement observes that vendor regulatory filings may not address some risks and that some risks only become apparent during use. This suggests a pre-purchase intake may catch documented hazards but may miss failure modes that surface after deployment, so intake review would likely need pairing with post-deployment monitoring.

The CHAI playbook requires vendors to complete a model card and standard intake application, and NIST AI 600-1 advises reviewing model and system cards for third-party models. A guidance document on augmented intelligence principles assigns liability to entities whose AI mandates prevent risk mitigation. None of these sources reports whether disclosure requirements change purchasing decisions.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures whether a standardized vendor intake changes which AI tools are purchased, how often vendors are declined or approved with compensating controls, how long review takes, or whether patient harm from AI tools falls afterward. A before-and-after or multi-site comparison of health systems with and without formal intake would address this.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from this evidence whether an intake process checks vendor performance in these groups, and safety-net organizations with limited governance staff have no data on the feasibility of adopting it.
